course.title: Network+ Capstone Branch
course.description: A branch office opens in six weeks with a network drawn on a napkin. Design it, build and prove it in Packet Tracer, operate it, then research the real equipment and plan the move.
course.audience: Design, build, operate and plan a real branch network as a four-person team — in Packet Tracer first, with no hardware needed to pass, then on borrowed kit if you can.

roles.name: Network Design (Design Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the design record: requirements, the addressing plan, the VLAN scheme and the map.

roles.name: Switching (Switch Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the switch record: VLANs, trunks, port security and every access port.

roles.name: Routing & Services (Router Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the router record: gateways, DHCP, DNS, NAT and the access list.

roles.name: Operations (Ops Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the operations record: logging, backups, changes, faults and the migration plan.

weeks.title: Preparation
weeks.theme: The simulator, a prompt, and the team
weeks.objective: Install Packet Tracer, reach a device prompt, register the lab path, and pick your focus.

objectives.label: Register the lab and the team

weeks.milestone: Packet Tracer opens, one switch answers at a prompt, and the register names the path, the version and the four focuses.

weeks.title: Design
weeks.objective: Discover what the branch needs, plan every subnet and VLAN, and build the empty topology in Packet Tracer.

objectives.label: Plan the addresses and the VLANs

weeks.milestone: The design brief traces every VLAN to a requirement, the IP plan is derived from one rule, and every device is placed and cabled.

weeks.title: Configure
weeks.objective: Configure the switches and the router so every VLAN gets an address, a gateway and a way out.
weeks.milestone: Every VLAN is on every switch, the trunks carry them, each gateway answers, a PC gets an address from DHCP, and a guest reaches the internet.

weeks.title: Operate
weeks.theme: Watch it, change it, break it, fix it
weeks.objective: Add logging, back up the configs, enforce the policy, make one change properly, and work three faults.

objectives.label: Watch it and back it up

weeks.milestone: Logs land in one place, every config is backed up, Guest is refused the practice, one change went through a record, and three faults are closed with the layer named.

weeks.title: Toward real equipment
weeks.objective: Research real equipment against the design, price a bill of materials, and write the migration plan.

objectives.label: Plan the move and hand over

weeks.milestone: Every device in the design has a researched real model with a checked capability, the bill of materials is priced from live listings, and the migration plan is issued.

weeks.title: On real kit
weeks.theme: The same build, on borrowed switches
weeks.objective: Run the Week 2 build on the CCNA kit if the team can borrow it, and record what differed.
weeks.milestone: The VLANs, trunk and gateways exist on real switches, and the differences from the simulator are a list.

tasks.title: Install the simulator and get to a prompt
tasks.objective: Install Packet Tracer, place one switch, open its console, and prove a prompt answers.
definitionOfDone: Packet Tracer opens and its version is in the register
One switch is placed and its CLI answers
The register says this build runs in the simulator

steps.title: Install Packet Tracer and record the version
steps.description: Packet Tracer opens, its version is in the register, and the path says simulator.
steps.instruction: Get Packet Tracer from Cisco Networking Academy with a free account, install it, and write the version into the register. Record that this build runs in the simulator.
steps.expectedOutput: Packet Tracer opens, its version is in the register, and the path says simulator.
instructionList: Skills for All or NetAcad: a free account gives the download.
Install, open, sign in once; it works offline afterwards.
Help, About: write the version in the register.

fixes.symptom: It asks to sign in every time?
fixes.fix: Sign in once with the account; guest mode limits saves. Record the account type in the register.

steps.whatItMeans: The simulator is simplified IOS. Knowing which version you ran is how a difference from real gear gets explained later.

steps.title: Place a switch and prove the prompt
steps.description: One switch on the canvas, its CLI open, two commands that answer.
steps.where: Packet Tracer — one switch, the CLI tab
steps.instruction: Drag a 2960 onto the canvas, open its CLI tab, press Enter, and run the two commands. Paste what the simulator prints.

commands.explain: From user mode to privileged mode. The prompt changes from > to #.
The simulated model and image. The register records it, model first.
commands.sample:
Cisco IOS Software, C2960 Software (C2960-LANBASEK9-M), Version 15.0(2)SE4, RELEASE SOFTWARE (fc1)
cisco WS-C2960-24TT-L (PowerPC405) processor (revision B0) with 65536K bytes of memory.

steps.whatItMeans: Everything in this course assumes you can type at a device. Prove it now, not in Week 2 when something else is also broken.
steps.expectedOutput:
Switch>enable
Switch#show version
Cisco IOS Software, C2960 Software (C2960-LANBASEK9-M), Version 15.0(2)SE4, RELEASE SOFTWARE (fc1)
cisco WS-C2960-24TT-L (PowerPC405) processor (revision B0) with 65536K bytes of memory.

tasks.title: Register the lab and the team
tasks.objective: Agree who leads which record, name the project file, and write the company brief the design starts from.
definitionOfDone: Each of the four focuses has a named member
One .pkt file is named and shared by the team
The brief is read and the open questions are listed

steps.title: Pick the focus and name the project file
steps.description: Four names against four focuses, one project file, and a list of questions the brief does not answer.
steps.instruction: Agree who leads Design, Switching, Routing and Operations. Save one project file named branch-t<team>.pkt and record where it lives. Read the brief: Millbrook Vets — Riverside branch.
steps.expectedOutput: Four names against four focuses, one project file, and a list of questions the brief does not answer.
steps.whatItMeans: A focus is the record a member leads, not the only work they do. Everyone configures and everyone pastes output.

tasks.title: Discover before you design
tasks.objective: Turn the brief into requirements: who needs what, what must never reach what, and what the building has.
definitionOfDone: Every group of users is a row with what it needs
The rules that separate groups are written as sentences
The building is surveyed: rooms, drops, where the router lands

steps.title: Write the requirements from the brief
steps.description: The brief has one row per group with its needs, and the rules are sentences a manager would sign.
steps.instruction: Read the brief and interview the business (your instructor plays it). One row per group: staff, printers, guests, the network team. Then the rules: what must never reach what.
steps.expectedOutput: The brief has one row per group with its needs, and the rules are sentences a manager would sign.
instructionList: 9 people on day one; count the devices, not the people.
Ask what cannot go down and for how long; that is the availability line.
Ask what a guest may reach. The answer is the first security rule.
steps.whatItMeans: A VLAN nobody can trace to a requirement is decoration. The rules written here become the access list in Week 3.

steps.title: Survey the building
steps.description: The survey names the cupboard, the drops per room, the ISP demarcation and the access point location.
steps.instruction: Walk the floor plan: the comms cupboard, the rooms, how many drops each needs, where the ISP router lands and where the guest access point goes. Record the constraints.
steps.expectedOutput: The survey names the cupboard, the drops per room, the ISP demarcation and the access point location.
steps.whatItMeans: The survey is why the design has two switches and not one: the consulting rooms are too far for one cabinet.

tasks.title: Plan the addresses and the VLANs
tasks.objective: One VLAN per group, one rule for every address, gateways and pools derived from it, and the management addresses fixed.
definitionOfDone: Every VLAN has an id, a name, a purpose and a prefix that follows the rule
Every pool leaves room for the static hosts
Every switch and the router have a management address

steps.title: Write the rule, then derive every subnet from it
steps.description: Four VLANs, each with a prefix, a gateway and a pool or a static note, all derived from the one rule.
steps.instruction: Adopt one rule: the third octet is the VLAN id, so Staff 10 is 10.70.10.0/24, gateway 10.70.10.1. Fill the VLAN table from the rule, never by typing.
steps.expectedOutput: Four VLANs, each with a prefix, a gateway and a pool or a static note, all derived from the one rule.
instructionList: Pools start at host 50 so the printers and switches below it are never handed out: Staff 10.70.10.50 – 10.70.10.199.
steps.whatItMeans: A rule is remembered; a spreadsheet of typed addresses is not. Every later command in this course follows this rule.

steps.title: Map every port before you touch a switch
steps.description: Every device in the design is on a port row, and the two trunks and the WAN link are named on both ends.
steps.instruction: One row per cabled port: switch, port, what plugs in, access or trunk, which VLAN. The two trunks and the ISP link are rows too.
steps.expectedOutput: Every device in the design is on a port row, and the two trunks and the WAN link are named on both ends.
steps.whatItMeans: Configuring first and documenting later is how the map and the switch end up different, usually on the port nobody checked.

tasks.title: Build the empty topology
tasks.objective: Place every device from the design, cable it exactly as the port map says, name each device, and prove the links are up.
definitionOfDone: Every device is placed with the model the design names
Every link in the port map exists, on the right ports, and is green
Every switch and the router carry their hostname

steps.title: Place and cable it as the map says
steps.description: Every device from the design is on the canvas and every link in the port map exists on its named ports.
steps.instruction: Place ISR 4321, two Catalyst 2960-24TT, the PCs, the printer, the access point and a cloud for the ISP. Cable each link on the exact ports in the map.
steps.expectedOutput: Every device from the design is on the canvas and every link in the port map exists on its named ports.
instructionList: Let the simulator pick the cable once, then redo one link by hand to learn which cable it chose.
Match the port names exactly; the map is what the configuration record will cite.
Label each device on the canvas with its hostname from the design.
steps.whatItMeans: A port that does not match the map is the first thing a fault hides behind in Week 3.

steps.title: Name the devices and prove the links
steps.description: Hostnames set, and every cabled port up on both switches.
steps.where: Packet Tracer — SW-01, the CLI tab
steps.instruction: Set each hostname from the design, then read the interface state and the neighbours on the first switch. Paste the output into the configuration record.

commands.explain: The name from the design, so every later paste says which device it came from.

commands.cmd: show ip interface brief | include up
commands.explain: Only the ports that are up. Each cabled port in the map should appear.
commands.sample:
FastEthernet0/1        unassigned      YES unset  up                    up
FastEthernet0/10       unassigned      YES unset  up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     unassigned      YES unset  up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/2     unassigned      YES unset  up                    up

commands.explain: What is on the other end of each uplink. The router and the second switch should both be listed.
commands.sample:
Device ID    Local Intrfce   Holdtme  Capability  Platform    Port ID
R1-BR        Gig 0/1         153      R           ISR4321     Gig 0/0/0
SW-02        Gig 0/2         167      S           2960        Gig 0/1

steps.whatItMeans: A green link and a neighbour on the far end is the proof the cabling matches the map before any VLAN exists.
steps.expectedOutput:
SW-01#show ip interface brief | include up
FastEthernet0/1        unassigned      YES unset  up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     unassigned      YES unset  up                    up

SW-01#show cdp neighbors
Device ID    Local Intrfce   Holdtme  Capability  Platform    Port ID
R1-BR        Gig 0/1         153      R           ISR4321     Gig 0/0/0
SW-02        Gig 0/2         167      S           2960        Gig 0/1

fixes.fix: Wrong cable type, or the port is shut. Replace the cable; on a router port run `no shutdown`.
Wait thirty seconds of simulation time; CDP announces on a timer. Then check the link is up at both ends.

tasks.title: Cut the switches into VLANs
tasks.objective: Create the four VLANs on both switches, put each access port where the map says, and trunk the switches and the router.
definitionOfDone: All four VLANs exist on both switches with the names from the plan
Every access port is in the VLAN the map says
Both trunks carry all four VLANs, native VLAN stated on both ends
Each switch answers on its management address

steps.title: Create the VLANs and place the access ports
steps.description: The VLAN table matches the plan, and each port sits where the map says.
steps.instruction: Create the four VLANs with their names, then put each access port in its VLAN. Read the table back and paste it into the record.

commands.cmd:
configure terminal
vlan 10
 name Staff
vlan 20
 name Devices
vlan 30
 name Guest
vlan 99
 name Management
end
commands.explain: The four VLANs with the names from the plan, so the table reads as the design does.

commands.cmd:
configure terminal
interface FastEthernet0/1
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
interface FastEthernet0/10
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 20
interface FastEthernet0/20
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 30
end
commands.explain: Each cabled access port in its VLAN, from the port map. Repeat on the second switch for its ports.
The table: every VLAN with its name and the ports in it. This is the proof.
commands.sample:
VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------
1    default                          active    Fa0/2, Fa0/3, Fa0/4, Fa0/5
10   Staff                            active    Fa0/1
20   Devices                          active    Fa0/10
30   Guest                            active    Fa0/20
99   Management                       active

steps.whatItMeans: A VLAN table that matches the plan on both switches is half of Week 2. The other half is the trunk that joins them.
steps.expectedOutput:
SW-01#show vlan brief
VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------
1    default                          active    Fa0/2, Fa0/3, Fa0/4, Fa0/5
10   Staff                            active    Fa0/1
20   Devices                          active    Fa0/10
30   Guest                            active    Fa0/20
99   Management                       active

outputHighlights.label: The VLAN exists with the name from the plan; the ports beside it are the access ports.

steps.title: Trunk the switches and the router, and address the management VLAN
steps.description: Two trunks carrying four VLANs, and a switch that answers on its own address.
steps.instruction: Make the two uplinks trunks with the native VLAN stated, give the switch its management address, and read the trunk list back.

commands.cmd:
configure terminal
interface range GigabitEthernet0/1 - 2
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
end
commands.explain: Both uplinks as 802.1Q trunks. The native VLAN is stated so the two ends can never disagree by default.

commands.cmd:
configure terminal
interface vlan 99
 ip address 10.70.99.11 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
ip default-gateway 10.70.99.1
end
commands.explain: The management interface, from the plan, and the gateway the network team reaches it through.
The trunks, their native VLAN and the VLANs they carry. All four should be listed as allowed and active.
commands.sample:
Port        Mode         Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gig0/1      on           802.1q         trunking      99
Gig0/2      on           802.1q         trunking      99

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gig0/1      1,10,20,30,99
Gig0/2      1,10,20,30,99

steps.whatItMeans: A native VLAN that differs on the two ends of a trunk is the classic fault. Stating it on both ends is the fix.
steps.expectedOutput:
SW-01#show interfaces trunk
Port        Mode         Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gig0/1      on           802.1q         trunking      99
Gig0/2      on           802.1q         trunking      99

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gig0/1      1,10,20,30,99
Gig0/2      1,10,20,30,99

fixes.symptom: A VLAN is allowed but not active on the trunk?
fixes.fix: It does not exist on this switch yet. Create it here too; a trunk only carries VLANs both ends know.

tasks.title: Route between them and out
tasks.objective: A subinterface per VLAN on the router over the trunk, a default route to the ISP, and NAT so the branch reaches the internet.
prerequisites: The trunks from the switch task
definitionOfDone: Every VLAN has a gateway on the router that answers a ping
The route table shows one connected route per VLAN and a default route
A staff PC reaches the ISP address through NAT

steps.title: Give every VLAN a gateway on one trunk
steps.description: Four subinterfaces, each with the gateway from the plan.
steps.where: Packet Tracer — R1-BR, the CLI tab
steps.instruction: Bring the inside interface up, create one subinterface per VLAN with 802.1Q tagging and the gateway address from the plan, then read the route table back.

commands.cmd:
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
 no shutdown
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 10.70.10.1 255.255.255.0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 20
 ip address 10.70.20.1 255.255.255.0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.30
 encapsulation dot1Q 30
 ip address 10.70.30.1 255.255.255.0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.99
 encapsulation dot1Q 99 native
 ip address 10.70.99.1 255.255.255.0
end
commands.explain: One subinterface per VLAN, tagged with its id, holding the gateway the plan derived. The management VLAN is the native one.
One connected route per VLAN. A VLAN missing here has no gateway.
commands.sample:
C        10.70.10.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0/0.10
C        10.70.20.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0/0.20
C        10.70.30.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0/0.30
C        10.70.99.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0/0.99

commands.explain: From a staff PC: the gateway answers, so the trunk, the tag and the subinterface all agree.

steps.whatItMeans: Router-on-a-stick is one trunk doing the work of four cables. A gateway that answers proves the tag matches on both ends.
steps.expectedOutput:
R1-BR#show ip route | include C 
C        10.70.10.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0/0.10
C        10.70.20.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0/0.20
C        10.70.30.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0/0.30
C        10.70.99.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0/0.99

steps.title: One way out: the default route and NAT
steps.description: The ISP link addressed, a default route, and the branch hidden behind one public address.
steps.where: Packet Tracer — R1-BR, the CLI tab
steps.instruction: Address the ISP interface from the plan, add the default route to the ISP, enable NAT overload for the inside VLANs, and prove it from a staff PC.

commands.cmd:
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.252
 ip nat outside
 no shutdown
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.10
 ip nat inside
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.20
 ip nat inside
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.30
 ip nat inside
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1
access-list 1 permit 10.70.0.0 0.0.255.255
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1 overload
end
commands.explain: The outside address, the way out, and NAT: every inside VLAN leaves as the router's public address.
From a staff PC. A reply means the default route and NAT both work; the ISP only ever sees the public address.
commands.sample:
Reply from 203.0.113.1: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=254
Reply from 203.0.113.1: bytes=32 time<1ms TTL=254

commands.explain: The translation the ping created: inside local, inside global. Empty means the ping did not pass through NAT.
commands.sample:
Pro  Inside global          Inside local           Outside local          Outside global
icmp 203.0.113.2:1          10.70.10.50:1          203.0.113.1:1          203.0.113.1:1

steps.whatItMeans: A branch with one public address is every small office. The translation table is the proof the design, not luck, got the packet out.
steps.expectedOutput:
C:\> ping 203.0.113.1
Reply from 203.0.113.1: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=254

R1-BR#show ip nat translations
Pro  Inside global          Inside local           Outside local          Outside global
icmp 203.0.113.2:1          10.70.10.50:1          203.0.113.1:1          203.0.113.1:1

fixes.symptom: The ping fails but the gateway answers?
fixes.fix: Three things, in order: the ISP interface is up, the default route exists in `show ip route`, and the subinterface carries `ip nat inside`.

tasks.title: Hand out addresses and names
tasks.objective: DHCP pools from the plan with the static hosts excluded, DNS passed through, and a client that proves it end to end.
definitionOfDone: A pool per client VLAN with the gateway and the DNS server set
The static hosts are excluded and the printer keeps its address
A staff PC and a guest get addresses from the right pools
The test matrix has a row per rule with its result

steps.title: Serve the pools from the plan
steps.description: Three pools, each with the gateway and the resolver, nothing below host 50.
steps.where: Packet Tracer — R1-BR, the CLI tab
steps.instruction: Exclude the static range in each VLAN, create a pool per client VLAN with its gateway and resolver, then set a PC to DHCP and read what it got.

commands.cmd:
configure terminal
ip dhcp excluded-address 10.70.10.1 10.70.10.49
ip dhcp pool STAFF
 network 10.70.10.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 10.70.10.1
 dns-server 203.0.113.53
ip dhcp excluded-address 10.70.20.1 10.70.20.49
ip dhcp pool DEVICES
 network 10.70.20.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 10.70.20.1
 dns-server 203.0.113.53
ip dhcp excluded-address 10.70.30.1 10.70.30.49
ip dhcp pool GUEST
 network 10.70.30.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 10.70.30.1
 dns-server 203.0.113.53
end
commands.explain: The static hosts excluded first, then one pool per client VLAN. The pool hands out the gateway and the resolver with the address.
On a staff PC set to DHCP. The address is in the pool, the gateway is the subinterface, the DNS server is the resolver.
On the router: the lease, with the client's hardware address. One row per client that asked.
commands.sample:
IP address       Client-ID/              Lease expiration        Type
                 Hardware address
10.70.10.50      0001.9647.3D1A          --                      Automatic
10.70.30.50      0002.4A11.B2C3          --                      Automatic

steps.whatItMeans: DHCP is where the design meets a real client. A wrong gateway in a pool looks exactly like a routing fault and wastes an afternoon.
steps.expectedOutput:
C:\> ipconfig /renew
   IPv4 Address......................: 10.70.10.50
   Default Gateway...................: 10.70.10.1
   DNS Server........................: 203.0.113.53

R1-BR#show ip dhcp binding
IP address       Client-ID/              Lease expiration        Type
10.70.10.50      0001.9647.3D1A          --                      Automatic

fixes.fix: The request never reached a pool. The port is in the wrong VLAN, the subinterface is down, or the pool's network does not match the VLAN prefix.

steps.title: Prove every rule in the test matrix
steps.description: One row per rule in the policy, each with a ping result and a reason.
steps.where: Packet Tracer — each PC, the Command Prompt
steps.instruction: From a staff PC and a guest, test each line of the policy: what should work and, for now, what still works but must not. Record each as a row.

commands.explain: From a staff PC: the printer answers, so Staff reaches Devices as the policy allows.
From the guest laptop: today this also answers, and the row says MUST FAIL. Week 3 makes it fail.
From a staff PC: the resolver the pool handed out answers a name.
commands.sample:
Server:  [203.0.113.53]
Address:  203.0.113.53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:    example.com
Address:  203.0.113.80

steps.whatItMeans: A test matrix with a row that says MUST FAIL and currently passes is an honest network. Week 3 closes it.
steps.expectedOutput:
C:\> ping 10.70.20.20
Reply from 10.70.20.20: bytes=32 time<1ms TTL=127

C:\> nslookup example.com
Server:  [203.0.113.53]
Name:    example.com
Address:  203.0.113.80

tasks.title: Watch it and back it up
tasks.objective: Send every device's logs to one place, set the clock, and save every running configuration off the device.
definitionOfDone: A syslog server receives a message from each device
Every device has the clock set and timestamps on
Each running configuration is saved to the server and named

steps.title: Logs to one place, with the time on them
steps.description: A server in the management VLAN receives a timestamped message from each device.
steps.where: Packet Tracer — a Server-PT in Management, then each device
steps.instruction: Add a server to the management VLAN with syslog on, point every device at it with timestamps enabled, and make one change so a message arrives.

commands.cmd:
configure terminal
service timestamps log datetime msec
logging host 10.70.99.10
logging trap informational
end
commands.explain: Every log line gets a time and goes to the server. Repeat on both switches and the router.
The device confirms where it sends. The server's address should be on the line.

steps.whatItMeans: A fault in Week 3 is found in the log first. A log with no timestamps is a story nobody can order.
steps.expectedOutput:
SW-01#show logging | include Logging to
    Logging to 10.70.99.10, 3 message lines logged

steps.title: Back up every configuration off the device
steps.description: Three files on the server, each named for its device and the date.
steps.where: Packet Tracer — each device, the CLI tab
steps.instruction: Turn TFTP on the server, copy each running configuration to it named device-date, and list what landed. Record the three names in the log.

commands.explain: The configuration as it runs now, to the server, under a name that says which device and when.
commands.sample:
Address or name of remote host [10.70.99.10]? 
Destination filename [SW-01-20261103.cfg]? 

Writing running-config...!!
[OK - 1342 bytes]

commands.explain: The one line that proves the file you copied was this device's.

steps.whatItMeans: A backup taken before the change is the way back. Week 3 changes nothing without one.
steps.expectedOutput:
SW-01#copy running-config tftp://10.70.99.10/SW-01-20261103.cfg
Writing running-config...!!
[OK - 1342 bytes]

fixes.fix: The server's TFTP service is off, or the switch has no management address in the same VLAN. Check both.

tasks.title: Enforce the policy
tasks.objective: Turn the written rules into an access list that refuses Guest the practice, and lock the access ports to one device each.
prerequisites: The test matrix rows marked MUST FAIL
definitionOfDone: Guest cannot reach Staff, Devices or Management, and still reaches the internet
Every MUST FAIL row in the matrix now fails, with the output pasted
Access ports accept one device and shut on a second

steps.title: Write the access list from the policy and prove the refusal
steps.description: Guest to the practice denied, Guest to the internet allowed, applied inbound on the guest subinterface.
steps.where: Packet Tracer — R1-BR, then the guest laptop
steps.instruction: Write the list from the policy table, apply it inbound on the Guest subinterface, then rerun the MUST FAIL rows from the guest and the MUST PASS rows from staff.

commands.cmd:
configure terminal
ip access-list extended GUEST-IN

DOMAINS.asks: Does this member hand work on cleanly, review others and hold their lane?
DOMAINS.evidence: The lifecycle rows with who moved what, the hand-offs and their forms, the peer review queue, the reports and the notes.

DOMAINS.label: Learning and retention
DOMAINS.definition: Skills proved on a second task, verified again a week or more later, reused in another course, and the pace month on month.
DOMAINS.asks: Is this member still learning, and keeping what was learned?
DOMAINS.evidence: The verification stamps of every skill: first and last, the tasks and courses between them, and the last two months of them.

DOMAINS.label: Professional readiness
DOMAINS.definition: The tier per record item at ten verified uses, the exam weight verified, the work-role coverage and the readiness score.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member consistently perform at a professional level in a real work environment?
DOMAINS.evidence: Every category of the record with its verified uses across courses, the published exam weights and the work roles’ required competencies.

KPIS.label: Skills verified
KPIS.numerator: Skills with at least one step verified from pasted output.
KPIS.denominator: Skills the role practises that carry a verifiable step.
KPIS.whyMember: Each verified skill names a task where the pasted output held every expected token.
KPIS.whyCompany: Skills backed by matched output rather than a tick, with the task behind each one named.

KPIS.label: Exam weight verified
KPIS.numerator: The published exam weight of every domain with a verified step, summed.
KPIS.denominator: The published exam weight of every domain the role practises, summed.
KPIS.whyMember: Shows which share of the exam blueprint the verified work already touches.
KPIS.whyCompany: Reads the verified work against the published exam domains and their weights.

KPIS.label: Commands verified
KPIS.numerator: Verified required steps that run a command.
KPIS.denominator: Verifiable required steps that run a command.
KPIS.whyMember: Command steps proven by their output; the table below splits them by tool.
KPIS.whyCompany: Tool use proven by output, per command step, split by tool in the table.

KPIS.label: Procedures to standard
KPIS.numerator: Followed procedures whose form cites a control code and was approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Procedures followed: every check due met and document control complete.
KPIS.whyMember: A runbook followed to a named control and approved by the team; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Procedures run to a cited NIST, ISO or SOC 2 control and approved by the team.

KPIS.label: Faults resolved
KPIS.numerator: Fault, incident and triage rows whose outcome column reads resolved.
KPIS.denominator: Fault, incident and triage rows the team filled on the forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Every fault the team logged, and how many ended resolved; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Troubleshooting success read from the fault and incident records the team kept.

KPIS.label: Verified after retry
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps that took more than one paste.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps.
KPIS.whyMember: A step that failed once and was then proven: the fault was found and fixed.
KPIS.whyCompany: How often a failed first paste was followed by a verified fix.

KPIS.label: Stuck flags cleared
KPIS.numerator: Stuck flags the member raised and later cleared.
KPIS.denominator: Stuck flags the member raised.
KPIS.whyMember: Asking for help and then getting past it both count; a flag never cleared says so.
KPIS.whyCompany: Blockers raised and worked through, from the append-only flag history.

KPIS.label: Time to resolution
KPIS.numerator: The median minutes from the first paste to the verification, per verified step with both stamps.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps with both stamps; the share within the hour is the percentage.
KPIS.whyMember: The median, so one long gap moves nothing; a step left over a day is counted apart.
KPIS.whyCompany: Minutes from first attempt to proof, read from two recorded stamps, never a clock.

KPIS.label: Steps verified in order
KPIS.numerator: Tasks whose verifiable steps were verified in the authored order.
KPIS.denominator: Tasks with two or more verification records, so an order exists.
KPIS.whyMember: The procedure was run as written, step after step.
KPIS.whyCompany: Runbooks followed in order, read from the sequence of verification records.

KPIS.label: First-try verifications
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps whose first paste held every expected token.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps.
KPIS.whyMember: Shown beside retries: a step verified after several pastes counts for as much.
KPIS.whyCompany: How often the first paste matched, printed beside how often it took more than one.

KPIS.label: Files named to convention
KPIS.numerator: Hashed files named to the evidence convention.
KPIS.denominator: Hashed files.
KPIS.whyMember: Evidence an auditor can find: date, team, tool and subject in every file name.
KPIS.whyCompany: Chain-of-custody hygiene: hashed files that follow the naming convention.

KPIS.label: Definition-of-Done met
KPIS.numerator: Definition-of-Done checks met on the forms of the role.
KPIS.denominator: Checks due on those forms through the current week.
KPIS.whyMember: Every check a form must pass this week, met or not, counted for the team.
KPIS.whyCompany: Work products measured against their own acceptance checks, week by week.

KPIS.label: Decisions recorded
KPIS.numerator: Decision blocks with an option chosen by this member.
KPIS.denominator: Decision blocks on the forms of the role, each with at least three options.
KPIS.whyMember: Each decision names the options weighed, the one chosen, who chose and when.
KPIS.whyCompany: Component, configuration and architecture choices made against named alternatives.

KPIS.label: Decisions justified
KPIS.numerator: Recorded decisions with every required supporting question answered.
KPIS.denominator: Decisions recorded by this member.
KPIS.whyMember: A choice with its reason, the rejected options and the risk accepted.
KPIS.whyCompany: Judgment shown in writing: rationale, rejected options, risk and rollback per decision.

KPIS.label: Decisions approved
KPIS.numerator: Recorded decisions on a form the team approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Decisions recorded by this member.
KPIS.whyMember: The team stood behind the choice; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Decisions that passed the team’s review and were issued.

KPIS.label: Changes with rollback
KPIS.numerator: Change-record rows with a rollback or back-out written.
KPIS.denominator: Change-record rows on the forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Every change the team logged, and how many had a way back written down first.
KPIS.whyCompany: Change discipline: a rollback plan on every recorded change.

KPIS.label: Hand-offs completed
KPIS.numerator: Hand-offs whose named deliverable reached approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Hand-offs of the tasks of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Work handed to another role that the team then approved or issued.
KPIS.whyCompany: Cross-role hand-offs closed by an approved document.

KPIS.label: RACI respected
KPIS.numerator: Lifecycle moves the member made in the role the RACI names for that move.
KPIS.denominator: Lifecycle moves the member made on forms with a RACI.
KPIS.whyMember: Submitting as the drafter, approving as the approver: the lane was held.
KPIS.whyCompany: Role discipline on documents, read from who moved what.

KPIS.label: Peer reviews given
KPIS.numerator: Blind peer reviews the member completed.
KPIS.denominator: Peer reviews assigned to the member.
KPIS.whyMember: Reviews of other teams’ frozen work, answered question by question.
KPIS.whyCompany: Review work done for others, from the blind review queue.

KPIS.label: Teammate steps ticked
KPIS.numerator: Required steps the member ticked on another role’s tasks.
KPIS.denominator: No denominator: a count.
KPIS.whyMember: Steps done on a teammate’s task, so a lane short of hands still finished.
KPIS.whyCompany: Help given across roles, counted in steps.

KPIS.label: On time
KPIS.numerator: Tasks whose last verification fell on or before the week due date.
KPIS.denominator: Tasks with a verification; needs the cohort start date.
KPIS.whyMember: The due date comes from the cohort calendar; without one the row says so.
KPIS.whyCompany: Reliability against a calendar, read from the verification stamps and the cohort start.

KPIS.label: Document control complete
KPIS.numerator: Forms with data whose document-control block is complete.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role with data.
KPIS.whyMember: Id, version, owner, date and status on every document the team filled.
KPIS.whyCompany: Document control kept on every filled form: id, version, owner, date, status.

KPIS.label: Controls cited
KPIS.numerator: Distinct control codes on approved or issued forms the role drafts.
KPIS.denominator: Distinct control codes the forms of the role cite.
KPIS.whyMember: The published controls the approved documents cite, by code.
KPIS.whyCompany: Control codes practised through approved documents, by standard.

KPIS.label: Instructor approved
KPIS.numerator: Forms of the role whose latest instructor review is approved.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Forms an instructor reviewed and approved; the latest review per form counts.
KPIS.whyCompany: Forms with an instructor verdict of approved, the latest review per form.

KPIS.label: Skills proved twice
KPIS.numerator: Skills with verified steps on two or more distinct tasks.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: A skill verified on two different tasks was carried from one context to another.
KPIS.whyCompany: Verification repeated on a second task is harder to reach by luck or by copying.

KPIS.label: Skills retained
KPIS.numerator: Skills verified again seven or more days after their first verification.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: Proof a week or more apart: the skill stayed.
KPIS.whyCompany: Retention read from the gap between two verification stamps on the same skill.

KPIS.label: Learning velocity
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before the page clock.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before those; the percentage caps at one hundred.
KPIS.whyMember: This month against last: rising, level or slowing, from the verification stamps.
KPIS.whyCompany: Pace of verified work, month on month, from recorded stamps.

KPIS.label: Profile coverage
KPIS.numerator: Required competencies of the selected work role or environment profile at verified or better.
KPIS.denominator: Required competencies the selected work role or environment profile names.
KPIS.whyMember: Measures the verified skills against a job role or a published company profile, with the untaught gap named.
KPIS.whyCompany: Coverage of the competencies a work role or an environment profile requires, read from verified steps.

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Technical capability
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: What the member can do: skills, commands and procedures proven by output against the exam and the role.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Can this member operate the tools and run the procedures the job needs?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Problem solving
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Faults logged and resolved, verifications reached after a failed paste, stuck flags cleared, and the minutes between first paste and proof.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: When something breaks, does this member find and fix it, and how long does it take?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Professional execution
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: How the work was done: steps in order, first pastes, evidence named to convention, every check due met.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member follow the runbook as written and leave evidence an auditor can find?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Decision making
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Decisions recorded against at least three options, justified, approved by the team, and changes with a rollback written.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member weigh options, say why, and plan the way back?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Teamwork
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected, peer reviews given and steps ticked on teammates’ tasks.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member hand work on cleanly and hold their lane in a team?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Professionalism
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: On time against the cohort calendar, documents controlled, controls cited, instructor approval earned.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member deliver on time, to standard, and to the reviewer’s satisfaction?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Growth
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Skills proved twice, retained across weeks, verified faster week on week, and the gap to a work role closing.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Is this member still learning, and keeping what was learned?

METRICS.label: Guide procedures followed

METRICS.label: Backup before write

METRICS.label: Procedures state-proven

METRICS.label: Tactics practised

METRICS.label: Technique ids cited

METRICS.definition: Engineering practices of tasks with at least one ticked step, over the practices the course maps.

METRICS.label: Practices verified
METRICS.definition: Practices of tasks with at least one verified step, over practices practised.

METRICS.label: Standards practised
METRICS.definition: Standards tagged on tasks or steps the member ticked, over standards the course tags.

METRICS.label: Effectiveness: forms
METRICS.definition: Per standard: forms citing it approved with all four rubric categories true, over forms citing it.

METRICS.label: Effectiveness: procedures
METRICS.definition: Per standard: SOP kinds anchored to it followed, over SOP kinds anchored to it.
METRICS.note: Loads on the course page.

METRICS.label: Controls cited

METRICS.note: Loads on the course page.

METRICS.label: Controls typed by member
METRICS.definition: Control codes the member typed into form fields that parse, over such fields.
METRICS.note: Team rows carry no author.

METRICS.label: Domains practised
METRICS.definition: Exam domains with at least one ticked task of the role, over domains the course practises.

METRICS.label: Domains verified
METRICS.definition: Exam domains with at least one verified step, over domains the course practises.

METRICS.label: Exam weight verified
METRICS.definition: Sum of the weights of verified domains over the weights the course practises.

METRICS.label: Next task per domain gap
METRICS.definition: The next task of the role that practises a domain not yet practised.

METRICS.label: Domain recall
METRICS.definition: A domain re-verified after a gap, over domains verified.

METRICS.definition: Verifiable required steps ticked without matching output, over verifiable required steps.

METRICS.label: Files named to convention

METRICS.label: Output proven on the lab
METRICS.definition: Steps whose output was verified on the lab, not in the browser, over verified steps.

METRICS.label: Time against estimate

METRICS.note: A team fact; loads on the course page.

METRICS.label: Ability estimate
METRICS.definition: A latent ability per objective estimated from item responses on a practice platform.
METRICS.note: The practice platform’s side; only a competency-level conclusion may cross, with consent.

METRICS.label: Readiness band
METRICS.definition: A pass-likelihood band per exam, validated against reported outcomes.
METRICS.note: The practice platform’s side; needs reported outcomes and consent.

METRICS.label: Transfer to unseen scenarios
METRICS.definition: Verified work on a scenario never practised before, over such scenarios.
METRICS.note: Needs scenario provenance per event.

METRICS.label: Unassisted verifications
METRICS.definition: Steps verified with no hint, tutor or agent assistance, over verified steps.
METRICS.note: Needs the assist level recorded per event.

METRICS.label: Rubric verdicts as events
METRICS.definition: The four category verdicts of each frozen submission, appended as events.
METRICS.note: The verdicts exist as rows today.

METRICS.label: Placement reported
METRICS.definition: Members who reported a role after a course, over members who answered with the outcome grant on.
METRICS.note: Counts only, shown from five answers; the employer name stays with the member.

METRICS.label: Used at work
METRICS.definition: Members who reported using a course at work, over members who answered with the outcome grant on.
METRICS.note: Self-reported by the member; an employer report needs a data agreement.

METRICS.label: Platform return
METRICS.definition: Cost per verified competency, and employer ramp saved, as the parties report them.
METRICS.note: Needs cost and employer data nobody has handed in.

METRICS.label: Time to competency
METRICS.definition: Days from the first verification of a skill to its tenth verified use.
METRICS.note: R132: the professional threshold is ten verified uses across courses.

METRICS.label: Task time against benchmark
METRICS.definition: Minutes to resolve a task against a published service-level baseline.
METRICS.note: R132: no baseline is published yet.

METRICS.label: Learning velocity
METRICS.definition: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before the page clock, over verified steps in the twenty-eight days before those.
METRICS.note: R132: the page passes the clock; the projection reads none.

PRACTICES.label: Default deny
PRACTICES.definition: Nothing passes a boundary unless a rule allows it; the allow list is the policy.

PRACTICES.label: Network segmentation
PRACTICES.definition: Zones with distinct trust levels are separated, and the flows between them are named and limited.

PRACTICES.label: Backup before change
PRACTICES.definition: A configuration is copied before it is edited, so the change can be reversed in one step.

PRACTICES.label: Change control
PRACTICES.definition: Every change is requested, reviewed, reversible and recorded before it reaches a system.

PRACTICES.label: Managed patching
PRACTICES.definition: Updates are inventoried, prioritised, tested, applied and verified on a cadence, not when something breaks.

PRACTICES.label: Hardening baseline
PRACTICES.definition: Hosts are configured to a written benchmark and checked against it, so drift from the baseline is visible.

PRACTICES.label: Configuration record
PRACTICES.definition: Every device configuration is saved, versioned and compared after a change.

PRACTICES.label: Build record
PRACTICES.definition: A build is recorded step by step with firmware, versions and settings as it is made.

PRACTICES.label: Centralised logging
PRACTICES.definition: Every host ships its logs to one place where they are kept, searched and alerted on.

PRACTICES.label: Lessons learned
PRACTICES.definition: After an incident or a drill, what worked and what did not is written down with an owner for each change.

PRACTICES.label: Written runbooks
PRACTICES.definition: Routine operations are written as steps a colleague could follow, and the steps are kept current.

PRACTICES.label: Sign and version documents
PRACTICES.definition: A document carries an id, a version, an owner, a date and a status, and a change makes a new version.

PRACTICES.label: As-built documentation
PRACTICES.definition: What was actually built is recorded, with addresses, versions and owners, and handed over with the system.

PRACTICES.label: Requirements before design
PRACTICES.definition: The design starts from written requirements and constraints, and each design element traces to one.

PRACTICES.label: Addressing plan
PRACTICES.definition: Subnets, addresses and names are planned on paper before any device is configured.

PRACTICES.label: Test and acceptance
PRACTICES.definition: A build is accepted against written tests with recorded results, not against a feeling that it works.

PRACTICES.label: Structured troubleshooting
PRACTICES.definition: Identify the problem, establish a theory, test it, plan and act, verify, document: in that order.

PRACTICES.label: Asset inventory
PRACTICES.definition: Every asset is listed with an owner, a location and a classification before it is protected.

PRACTICES.label: Work tracked on a board
PRACTICES.definition: Every task of the week is a card with an owner and a state on the team board.

SCORING.label: Tool proficiency
SCORING.definition: Commands and skills proven by output, and skills proved on a second task, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Reads browser checks and receipts of stamps, not proof of the machine; the per-tool table names each command.

SCORING.label: Troubleshooting success
SCORING.definition: Faults resolved, retries that verified, stuck flags cleared and steps resolved within the hour, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Faults are team rows; the minutes are a median between two recorded stamps, so a step left open overnight is counted apart.

SCORING.label: Judgment
SCORING.definition: Decisions recorded, justified and approved, and changes with a rollback written, equally weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Counts what was written against named options; it does not judge whether the choice was right.

SCORING.label: Collaboration
SCORING.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected and peer reviews given, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Team facts count for the team; the role share on the KPIs says what this member moved.

SCORING.label: Reliability
SCORING.definition: On time against the cohort calendar, document control complete, controls cited and instructor approval, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: On time needs the cohort start date; without one the score stands on the other three and says so.

SCORING.label: Readiness
SCORING.definition: Exam weight verified, work-role coverage, skills retained and steps in order, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: A reading of the record against an exam and a work role, not a prediction of a pass or a hire.

SOPS.label: Incident record
SOPS.definition: The record of one incident: first alert, attacker, timeline, containment time, evidence and the hand-offs.

SOPS.label: Change record
SOPS.definition: A change written before it is made: what, where, the backup, the approval, the rollback and the result.

SOPS.label: Backup plan
SOPS.definition: What is backed up, how often, where it goes, how long it is kept and how a restore is tested.

SOPS.label: Chain of custody
SOPS.definition: Every evidence item logged with its hash, who held it, when, and where it is stored.

SOPS.label: Hardening baseline
SOPS.definition: The settings a host must have, the benchmark they come from, and the proof each host meets them.

SOPS.label: Operational handover
SOPS.definition: What was built, how it is run, who owns it and what is still open, handed to the next team.

SOPS.label: Asset inventory

SOPS.label: Network design

SOPS.label: Requirements record
SOPS.definition: What the system must do and must not, with the constraints and the acceptance criteria.

SOPS.label: Build record

SOPS.label: Test and acceptance record
SOPS.definition: The tests a build must pass, who ran them, and the recorded results.

STANDARDS.label: NIST CSF
STANDARDS.description: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
STANDARDS.why: Organises all security work into six functions. Tagging a step here shows which part of the lifecycle it strengthens and proves the work covered the whole picture, not just attack or defence.

STANDARDS.label: CIS
STANDARDS.description: CIS Critical Security Controls v8 and the CIS Benchmarks
STANDARDS.why: A prioritised "do these first" list of safeguards. A CIS tag means this step implements an industry-baseline control that auditors and blue teams recognise at once.

STANDARDS.label: NIST 800-61
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-61 Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
STANDARDS.why: The incident-handling playbook: prepare, detect and analyse, contain, eradicate, recover, learn. This tag means the step is part of a defensible, court-ready incident response process.

STANDARDS.label: ISO 27001
STANDARDS.why: The certifiable information security management standard. This tag means the step produces the documented policy or evidence an ISO 27001 audit expects to see.

STANDARDS.label: SOC 2
STANDARDS.description: AICPA Trust Services Criteria for a SOC 2 examination
STANDARDS.why: The AICPA attestation standard built on the Trust Services Criteria: Security is CC1 to CC9, plus Availability, Confidentiality and the rest. This tag means the step produces a control or the evidence a SOC 2 Type I or II examiner samples.

STANDARDS.label: Network+ N10-009
STANDARDS.description: CompTIA Network+ N10-009: the exam blueprint and its five domains
STANDARDS.why: The Network+ blueprint: concepts, implementation, operations, security and troubleshooting. This tag says which exam domain the work covers, so the portfolio and the syllabus can be read against each other.

STANDARDS.label: ITIL 4
STANDARDS.description: ITIL 4 service management practices: change, incident, problem, release
STANDARDS.why: The operating disciplines a network team is judged on: change, incident and problem management. A tag here means the step is not just technically right but done the way an organisation can audit: requested, reviewed, reversible and recorded.

STANDARDS.label: Well-Architected
STANDARDS.description: Well-Architected Framework pillars, Azure and AWS
STANDARDS.why: Both clouds judge a design on the same pillars: reliability, security, cost, operational excellence and performance. A tag here means the step is a design choice one of them would ask about.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-53
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 security and privacy controls
STANDARDS.why: The federal control catalogue the sixteen CISSP control statements are drawn from (PM-1, SC-7, AC-2). A tag here means the step writes or proves one of those controls.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-40
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-40 Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning
STANDARDS.why: Patching as a managed routine rather than a scramble: inventory, prioritise, test, deploy, verify. A vulnerability management SOP that cites it has a defensible cadence.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC 27037
STANDARDS.description: ISO/IEC 27037 identification, collection, acquisition and preservation of digital evidence
STANDARDS.why: How evidence is collected and kept so it still counts later: identify, collect, acquire, preserve, with a chain of custody. An evidence log that cites it can be trusted in a dispute.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010
STANDARDS.why: What an architecture description must contain: stakeholders, concerns, viewpoints and the decisions behind them. A solution architecture document that cites it is complete rather than a diagram.

CUSTODY_RULES: Preserve the original — work on copies; never edit or rename the original artifact after collection.
Name every artifact `YYYYMMDD_TeamXX_Tool_Action.ext` so it is dated, attributed and self-describing.
Hash on collection: `sha256sum <file> >> Evidence_Hashes.txt`. Verify on receipt/before reporting: `sha256sum -c Evidence_Hashes.txt`.
Log every artifact in this file the moment it is collected — and log every hand-off (who → who, when).
Keep every artifact for a week in `~/team-artifacts/week-N/`; the team package gathers them into `04_Testing_and_Findings/Evidence/`. Keep originals read-only and backed up.
One custodian holds the evidence at a time; record each transfer so the chain is unbroken.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The terminal doesn’t recognise the program — usually a typo or the tool isn’t installed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the spelling. If it’s really missing, install it: sudo apt update && sudo apt install <tool>

variants.otherwise: — the step that first uses a tool says how to install it.

ERROR_ROWS.fix: Add sudo in front on Linux (sudo <command>). On Windows/PowerShell, close it and reopen with “Run as administrator”.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Connection refused / No route to host / host seems down
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You can’t reach the target — it’s off, the IP is wrong, or you’re not on the right network.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: ping the address first. Confirm the machine is powered on and that you are on the same subnet as it

variants.then: , and that you set the right IP in Lab access.
variants.otherwise: — a host in another zone only answers once the route between them exists.

variants.then: For nmap, add -Pn to scan a host that blocks ping.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You’re in the wrong folder, or the path/filename is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run pwd to see where you are and cd ~ to go home.

variants.then: For hydra, rockyou is gzipped by default — unzip it once: sudo gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz
variants.otherwise: Check the file really exists with ls before you edit it — a config path is easy to mistype.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: That’s a placeholder, not a real address — you copied it literally.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Open the Lab access panel at the top of the Tasks tab and enter {label}; the site then fills it into every command automatically.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: ssh: connect to host … Operation timed out (from home)
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Your laptop is not on the tailnet, or the host is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the Tailscale client is signed in and connected on your laptop, then run tailscale status on the host — it must list the host as online. On campus you can still reach it on its 10.10.30.T address while you sort this out.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: The Proxmox console times out but SSH works
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The path is fine; the web service or the port is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run systemctl status pveproxy --no-pager over SSH. Remember the console is on port 8006 and https, not http — a plain http:// URL simply hangs.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: It worked yesterday and not today
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The host rebooted and something did not come back, or your address changed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: systemctl is-active tailscaled on the host must read active. The host keeps the same Tailscale address across reboots, so if the address you saved has changed, you are looking at a rebuilt host that was re-authorised as a new device.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Permission denied (publickey) after setting up keys
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The key is not where the server expects it, or the account is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run ssh -v to see which key is offered, and confirm you are connecting as the right user. Password login is still enabled until Week 4 hardens it, so you have a way back in — use it rather than locking yourself out further.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The VM cannot reach the Core over the ops network — the second NIC, the VLAN tag or the bridge is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: On the host, ip -br a must show vmbr9 UP with the team’s 10.20.T.1 address. Inside the VM, the second interface needs its 10.20.T.x address and no gateway. Still nothing: the switch port is not trunking VLAN 20 — the Networking deep-dive owns that.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Some commands (a bare ping, a large download, a package install) run until you stop them, or they’re waiting on a slow or unreachable host.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Press Ctrl+C to stop it. Re-check reachability (ping), and give a genuinely long job a minute

variants.otherwise: — an OS install or a big apt upgrade takes minutes, not seconds.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: When anything fails, the error’s last line usually names the real problem.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Match that line to the rows above. Also double-check you’re on the machine the step’s WHERE chip names — running the right command on the wrong host is the most common cause.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Open a terminal
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: On a Linux desktop, click the black terminal icon or press Ctrl+Alt+T. On a server you reach over SSH, the terminal is the session itself. You type commands here and press Enter to run them.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: The prompt
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: A line ending in $ (or #) is the prompt — it means the terminal is waiting for you. You don’t type the $ itself.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Paste a command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Copy from this site, then in the terminal press Ctrl+Shift+V (plain Ctrl+V often does nothing in a terminal). Right-click → Paste also works.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Run one line at a time
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: When a step shows several numbered commands, run them one by one — paste one, press Enter, wait for it to finish, then the next.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: sudo = run as admin
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: sudo runs a command with admin rights (it may ask for your password — typing shows nothing, that’s normal). On Windows/PowerShell, instead right-click PowerShell → “Run as administrator”.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Stop a stuck command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Press Ctrl+C to cancel a command that hangs or runs forever (e.g. a ping with no -c limit).

TERMINAL_COPY.intro: New to the command line? These are the only things you need to know to run every command in this course.
